pfl.grundsatz.0: What counts is what the person can do themselves, not what they are doing right now or whether someone does it for them out of habit.
pfl.grundsatz.1: Aids such as a walker, grab bar or glasses count as “alone”: only help from other people is assessed.
pfl.grundsatz.2: Think of a completely normal day, including bad days if they happen often. What counts is how it has been in recent months and will stay for at least six more months.
pfl.grundsatz.3: Honest rather than high: the estimate only helps with the application and the appointment with the assessor if the answers are true.
pfl.kind: For children, the assessor compares with a healthy child of the same age. What a child of that age cannot do anyway does not count.
pfl.vorfrage.1.0: Does the person have problems moving?
pfl.vorfrage.1.1: For example getting up, moving from bed to chair, walking in the home or on the stairs.
pfl.vorfrage.2.0: Does the person have problems understanding, remembering or finding their way?
pfl.vorfrage.2.1: For example with dementia, intellectual disability or after a stroke: recognising people, knowing the day of the week, understanding conversations.
pfl.vorfrage.3.0: Is there behaviour or are there feelings where someone has to step in, calm the person or keep watch?
pfl.vorfrage.3.1: For example restlessness at night, running away, fears, aggression, resisting care or severe lack of drive.
pfl.vorfrage.4.0: Does the person need help with washing, dressing, eating, drinking or using the toilet?
pfl.vorfrage.4.1: Reminding, guiding or laying things out is also help.
pfl.vorfrage.5.0: Does the person need help with medication, measurements, wounds, therapies or doctor's visits?
pfl.vorfrage.5.1: This means help because the person cannot do it themselves, for example preparing tablets, measuring blood sugar or going with them to the doctor.
pfl.vorfrage.6.0: Does the person need help organising their day or keeping in touch with others?
pfl.vorfrage.6.1: For example planning the daily routine, keeping busy, sleeping, phoning or receiving visitors.
pfl.text.1.1.0: Can the person turn over in bed and sit up alone?
pfl.text.1.1.1: Counts: turning from the back onto the side, moving up in bed, getting from lying to sitting. A bed hoist or a rope ladder counts as an aid.
pfl.text.1.2.0: Can the person stay sitting upright alone?
pfl.text.1.2.1: Counts: sitting on a chair or the edge of the bed without tipping to the side. Someone who only needs to support themselves with their arms is still sitting alone.
pfl.text.1.3.0: Can the person move from the bed to a chair and back alone?
pfl.text.1.3.1: Also counts: from the wheelchair onto the toilet or getting up from an armchair. If someone has to support, hold or lift, that is help.
pfl.text.1.4.0: Can the person walk from room to room in the home alone?
pfl.text.1.4.1: With a walker or a wheelchair that the person moves themselves, this counts as alone. Does not count: walking outside on the street.
pfl.text.1.5.0: Can the person climb stairs between two floors alone?
pfl.text.1.5.1: What matters is the ability, even if there are no stairs at home. Someone who only holds on to the handrail walks alone; someone who has to be supported or carried does not.
pfl.text.2.1.0: Does the person recognise familiar people?
pfl.text.2.1.1: For example family, neighbours or the carer who comes regularly. It is about recognising, not remembering the name.
pfl.text.2.2.0: Does the person know where they are, and can they find their way around the home?
pfl.text.2.2.1: For example: finds the bathroom, knows they are at home, finds the way back when outside.
pfl.text.2.3.0: Does the person know the time of day, the day and the season?
pfl.text.2.3.1: Someone who now and then mixes up the day of the week is still largely oriented. If the person mixes up day and night, the ability is severely limited.
pfl.text.2.4.0: Can the person remember important things?
pfl.text.2.4.1: For example: what there was for lunch, whether there were visitors, important events in their life.
pfl.text.2.5.0: Can the person manage tasks with several steps in the right order?
pfl.text.2.5.1: For example: getting dressed in the right order, making coffee, buttering bread. If someone has to announce every step, the ability is hardly present.
pfl.text.2.6.0: Can the person make sensible decisions in everyday life on their own?
pfl.text.2.6.1: For example: choosing clothes suitable for the weather, deciding what they want to eat or do.
pfl.text.2.7.0: Does the person understand what is happening around them and what is explained to them?
pfl.text.2.7.1: For example: do they understand why the doctor is coming or that an appointment is coming up?
pfl.text.2.8.1: For example a hot hob, an open window, road traffic, spoiled food, tripping hazards.
pfl.text.2.9.0: Can the person say or show when they need something?
pfl.text.2.9.1: For example hunger, thirst, pain, feeling cold or needing the toilet. Gestures and sounds also count.
pfl.text.2.10.0: Does the person understand simple requests?
pfl.text.2.10.1: For example “Please sit down” or “Raise your arm”. A hearing aid counts as an aid.
pfl.text.2.11.0: Can the person follow a conversation and take part?
pfl.text.2.11.1: For example during a visit or on the phone: answering questions, staying on topic.
pfl.text.3.1.0: How often does someone have to step in because the person wanders around, does not stay seated or wants to run away?
pfl.text.3.1.1: For all questions in this area, what counts is how often someone has to step in, calm the person or keep watch, not how often the behaviour occurs.
pfl.text.3.2.0: How often does the person need help at night because they are awake and restless?
pfl.text.3.2.1: Counts: getting up at night and wandering around, mixing up day and night, waking someone. Does not count: just sleeping badly without help from others.
pfl.text.3.3.0: How often does someone have to stop the person from hurting themselves?
pfl.text.3.3.1: For example scratching, hitting or biting themselves, eating or drinking dangerous things.
pfl.text.3.4.0: How often does someone have to step in because the person breaks or throws away things?
pfl.text.3.4.1: For example smashing dishes, tearing clothes, throwing objects out of the window.
pfl.text.3.5.0: How often does the person physically attack others?
pfl.text.3.5.1: For example hitting, kicking, scratching, pushing or throwing objects.
pfl.text.3.6.0: How often does the person insult or threaten others?
pfl.text.3.6.1: Counts if someone has to react and calm the person.
pfl.text.3.7.0: How often does the person call out, scream or keep repeating something, so that someone has to react?
pfl.text.3.7.1: For example loud calling, complaining, constant asking or repeating sentences.
pfl.text.3.8.0: How often does the person resist care or help?
pfl.text.3.8.1: For example when washing, dressing, eating or taking medication, so that you have to try several times or persuade them.
pfl.text.3.9.0: How often does someone have to help because the person sees or believes things that are not real?
pfl.text.3.9.1: For example they believe they are being robbed or followed, or see people who are not there.
pfl.text.3.10.0: How often does the person have strong fears where someone has to calm them?
pfl.text.3.10.1: For example fear of being alone, panic without any recognisable reason.
pfl.text.3.11.0: How often does the person have to be prompted and motivated because they lack drive and are depressed?
pfl.text.3.11.1: For example: does not get up without being asked, does not eat, does not wash, withdraws completely.
pfl.text.3.12.0: How often does the person behave so inappropriately that someone has to step in?
pfl.text.3.12.1: For example undressing in public, touching strangers, lacking any sense of distance.
pfl.text.3.13.0: How often does the person do other inappropriate things where someone has to step in?
pfl.text.3.13.1: For example hiding or hoarding things, smearing faeces, putting food in the wardrobe.
pfl.text.4.1.0: Can the person wash their hands, face, arms, chest and belly alone?
pfl.text.4.1.1: Reminding, handing over the flannel or guiding is also help.
pfl.text.4.2.0: Can the person comb their hair, brush their teeth and shave alone?
pfl.text.4.2.1: Cleaning dentures is also part of this.
pfl.text.4.3.0: Can the person wash their intimate area alone?
pfl.text.4.3.1: This also counts if it is embarrassing to talk about. An honest answer is especially important here.
pfl.text.4.4.0: Can the person shower or bathe and wash their hair alone?
pfl.text.4.4.1: Also counts: getting into and out of the shower or bath. A bath lift counts as an aid.
pfl.text.4.5.0: Can the person put on and take off a shirt, jumper or bra alone?
pfl.text.4.5.1: Laying out clothes, doing up buttons or reminding of the order is also help.
pfl.text.4.6.0: Can the person put on and take off trousers, underwear, socks and shoes alone?
pfl.text.4.6.1: Compression stockings do not belong here but to area 5.
pfl.text.4.7.0: Can the person cut up food, butter bread and pour drinks alone?
pfl.text.4.7.1: Does not count: cooking and shopping.
pfl.text.4.8.1: Bringing food to the mouth, chewing and swallowing. If someone has to keep prompting the person to eat, that is also help. This question counts three times.
pfl.text.4.9.0: Does the person drink alone and enough?
pfl.text.4.9.1: If someone has to keep prompting the person to drink or hand them the glass, that is help. This question counts twice.
pfl.text.4.10.0: Can the person go to the toilet alone and clean themselves afterwards?
pfl.text.4.10.1: Counts: getting there, sitting down, adjusting clothes, wiping, flushing. Also commode, urine bottle or bedpan. This question counts twice.
pfl.text.4.11.0: Can the person change pads or look after a catheter or urostomy alone?
pfl.text.4.11.1: Only asked if the person is mostly or completely incontinent or has a catheter or a urostomy.
pfl.text.4.12.0: With faecal incontinence, can the person clean themselves or look after a stoma alone?
pfl.text.4.12.1: Only asked if the person is mostly or completely faecally incontinent or has an artificial bowel outlet.
pfl.text.4.13.1: Only important if a feeding tube or drip is needed. “Tube in addition to food” gives more points than “almost only by tube”, because then help with normal eating is needed as well.
pfl.text.6.1.0: Can the person plan their day themselves and cope with changes?
pfl.text.6.1.1: For example knowing when to get up, eat and go to bed, and coping with a rescheduled appointment.
pfl.text.6.2.0: Can the person settle down and sleep alone?
pfl.text.6.2.1: Counts: going to bed, falling asleep, sleeping through. If someone has to help at night, calm the person or reposition them, that is help.
pfl.text.6.3.0: Can the person keep themselves meaningfully occupied alone?
pfl.text.6.3.1: For example reading, watching TV, listening to music, handicrafts. If someone has to offer and guide activities, that is help.
pfl.text.6.4.0: Can the person plan something for the next few days themselves?
pfl.text.6.4.1: For example remembering a doctor's appointment or getting ready for visitors at the weekend.
pfl.text.6.5.0: Does the person get along alone with people around them?
pfl.text.6.5.1: For example greeting visitors, dealing with housemates, reacting to others.
pfl.text.6.6.0: Can the person keep in touch with friends and relatives alone?
pfl.text.6.6.1: For example phoning, writing messages, arranging to meet.
pfl.m5.5.1: Does someone have to prepare or give the medication?
pfl.m5.5.2: Does someone have to give injections, for example insulin?
pfl.m5.5.3: Does someone have to look after a port or venous access?
pfl.m5.5.4: Does someone have to do suction or give oxygen?
pfl.m5.5.5: Does someone have to apply ointments or use cold or warm packs?
pfl.m5.5.6: Does someone have to measure and interpret blood sugar, blood pressure or weight?
pfl.m5.5.7: Does someone have to put on compression stockings, a prosthesis, a hearing aid or glasses?
pfl.m5.5.8: Does someone have to change dressings or care for wounds?
pfl.m5.5.9: Does someone have to look after a stoma?
pfl.m5.5.10: Does someone have to insert a disposable catheter or help with bowel movements?
pfl.m5.5.11: Does someone have to do exercises from physiotherapy or speech therapy with the person at home?
pfl.m5.5.12: Does the person need complex treatment at home, such as home ventilation or dialysis, where someone helps?
pfl.m5.5.13: Does someone have to accompany the person to the doctor?
pfl.m5.5.14: Does someone have to accompany the person to physiotherapy or another therapy (up to 3 hours)?
pfl.m5.5.15: Does someone have to accompany the person to long treatments, for example dialysis or chemotherapy (more than 3 hours)?
pfl.m5.5.K: Does someone have to accompany the child to early intervention (Frühförderung)?
pfl.m5.5.16: Can the person keep to a diet or medical instructions alone?
pfl.m5Kurz.5.3: Looking after a port or venous access
pfl.m5Kurz.5.5: Applying creams, cold or warm packs
pfl.m5Kurz.5.6: Measuring blood sugar, blood pressure or weight
pfl.m5Kurz.5.7: Putting on compression stockings, prosthesis, hearing aid or glasses
pfl.m5Kurz.5.10: Inserting a disposable catheter or helping with bowel movements
pfl.m5Kurz.5.11: Exercises from physiotherapy or speech therapy at home
pfl.m5Kurz.5.12: Complex treatment at home, for example home ventilation or dialysis
pfl.m5Kurz.5.14: Accompanying to therapy, for example physiotherapy (up to 3 hours)
pfl.m5Kurz.5.15: Accompanying to long treatments, for example dialysis or chemotherapy (more than 3 hours)
pfl.m5Tipp.5.1: For example putting tablets into the pill organiser, giving drops, reminding them to take them and making sure they really are taken.
pfl.m5Tipp.5.6: For example measuring blood sugar before meals and adjusting the amount of insulin accordingly.
pfl.m5Tipp.5.7: Only putting on and taking off counts. Compression stockings on in the morning and off in the evening are twice a day.
pfl.m5Tipp.5.13: Counts if the person cannot go there alone but has to be accompanied or taken.
pfl.m5Tipp.5.16: For example a diabetes diet, fluid amounts for heart failure or restrictions after an operation.
pfl.m5Hinweis: Only counts if someone else helps because the person cannot do it themselves. If the person does it themselves, the answer is “No”.
pfl.m5Oft.5.1: How often does someone have to prepare or give the medication?
pfl.m5Oft.5.2: How often does someone have to give injections, for example insulin?
pfl.m5Oft.5.3: How often does someone have to look after a port or venous access?
pfl.m5Oft.5.4: How often does someone have to do suction or give oxygen?
pfl.m5Oft.5.5: How often does someone have to apply ointments or use cold or warm packs?
pfl.m5Oft.5.6: How often does someone have to measure and interpret blood sugar, blood pressure or weight?
pfl.m5Oft.5.7: How often does someone have to put on compression stockings, a prosthesis, a hearing aid or glasses?
pfl.m5Oft.5.8: How often does someone have to change dressings or care for wounds?
pfl.m5Oft.5.9: How often does someone have to look after a stoma?
pfl.m5Oft.5.10: How often does someone have to insert a disposable catheter or help with bowel movements?
pfl.m5Oft.5.11: How often does someone have to do exercises from physiotherapy or speech therapy with the person at home?
pfl.m5Oft.5.12: How often is the complex treatment at home needed?
pfl.m5Oft.5.13: How often does someone have to accompany the person to the doctor?
pfl.m5Oft.5.14: How often does someone have to accompany the person to physiotherapy or another therapy (up to 3 hours)?
pfl.m5Oft.5.15: How often does someone have to accompany the person to long treatments, for example dialysis or chemotherapy (more than 3 hours)?
pfl.m5Oft.5.K: How often does someone have to accompany the child to early intervention (Frühförderung)?
pfl.antworten.sel.2: manages only a small part alone
pfl.antworten.sel.3: cannot manage it alone at all
pfl.antworten.hfg.1: once to three times in 2 weeks
pfl.antworten.oft.4: 4 times a day or more often
pfl.antworten.aufwendig.0: On some days of the week
pfl.ui.alter.frage: How old is the person who is cared for?
pfl.ui.sogehts.1: There are 6 areas of life. Each starts with a yes-or-no question.
pfl.ui.sogehts.2: More detailed questions follow only after “Yes”. Under each question it says what counts.
pfl.ui.sogehts.3: At the end you see which care level (Pflegegrad) is likely.
pfl.ui.sogehts.klein: Only help from other people counts. Aids such as a walker or glasses count as “alone”. You can stop at any time.
pfl.ui.alter.warn: Please enter the age in years.
pfl.ui.k4K.frage: Are there such big problems with feeding that care is exceptionally demanding?
pfl.ui.k4K.hinweis: Only for children up to 18 months: this means, for example, swallowing problems, very long meals or feeding by tube.
pfl.ui.ink.frage: Is the person incontinent, or do they have a catheter or a stoma?
pfl.ui.ink.hinweis: This means mostly or completely incontinent, so more than a few drops now and then.
pfl.ui.m5liste.frage: What does someone have to help with?
pfl.ui.m5liste.hinweis: Tap everything that applies. It only counts if someone else helps because the person cannot do it themselves. After that we ask how often only for these points.
pfl.ui.erg.hinweis: This is an estimate. The decision is made by the care insurance fund (Pflegekasse).
pfl.ui.erg.hoeher: You now have care level (Pflegegrad) {jetzt}. According to your estimate, care level {pg} could apply. An application for a higher level (Höherstufung) is probably worthwhile.
pfl.ui.erg.gleich: That matches your current care level (Pflegegrad) {jetzt}. According to this estimate, a higher level is not yet worthwhile.
pfl.ui.erg.niedriger: The estimate is below your current care level (Pflegegrad) {jetzt}. Do not apply for a higher level (Höherstufung) without advice: the Pflegekasse then checks again and may also grade lower.
pfl.ui.erg.knapp: It is close: {f} points are missing for care level (Pflegegrad) {pg}. Check the answers you were unsure about.
pfl.ui.erg.fehlt: {f} points are missing for care level (Pflegegrad) {pg}.
pfl.ui.erg.grenzen: From 12.5 points there is care level 1, from 27 care level 2, from 47.5 care level 3, from 70 care level 4, from 90 care level 5. Of areas 2 and 3, only the higher one counts (§ 15 SGB XI).
pfl.ui.erg.tippTitel: Tip for the appointment with the assessor
pfl.ui.erg.tipp: Keep a care diary for a week: what was needed, how often, for how long? Have doctor's reports and the medication plan ready for the appointment, and be there if possible. Do not show better sides than in everyday life.
pfl.ui.bed.geld: Care allowance (Pflegegeld): {b} a month into the account if relatives provide care
pfl.ui.bed.dienst: Or a home care service: up to {b} a month, the Pflegekasse pays directly
pfl.ui.bed.entl: Relief amount (Entlastungsbetrag): {b} a month for help in everyday life, no money into the account
pfl.ui.bed.vorweg1: With care level (Pflegegrad) 1 there is no care allowance (Pflegegeld) yet, but there is this help from the Pflegekasse:
pfl.ui.bed.hilfs: Care aids such as gloves: up to {b} a month
pfl.ui.bed.umbau: Adapting the home: up to {b} per measure
pfl.ui.bed.kein1: Without a care level (Pflegegrad) there is no money from the Pflegekasse.
pfl.ui.bed.kein2: Care advice and care courses for relatives are free of charge.
pfl.pu.geld.x: Paid into the account if relatives, friends or neighbours provide care. The person cared for decides freely what to use it for.
pfl.pu.geld.m0: With care levels 4 and 5 this is also possible every quarter on request.
pfl.pu.geld.w: With Pflegegeld, a free compulsory advice visit comes to the home once every six months. If it does not take place, the care insurance fund (Pflegekasse) can reduce the Pflegegeld.
pfl.pu.dienst.t: A care service comes to the home (Pflegesachleistung)
pfl.pu.dienst.x: No money into the account: the care service bills the Pflegekasse directly up to this amount.
pfl.pu.dienst.m0: Possible instead of Pflegegeld or together with it (see “Care service and Pflegegeld combined”).
pfl.pu.dienst.m1: What the care service does not need in a month, you can also use for recognised help in everyday life, up to 40 % of the amount (conversion, Umwandlung). You submit the invoices to the Pflegekasse.
pfl.pu.entl.t: Money for help in everyday life (Entlastungsbetrag)
pfl.pu.entl.x: No money into the account: the Pflegekasse uses it to pay invoices from recognised providers, for example for household help, supervision or accompaniment.
pfl.pu.entl.pg1: With care level (Pflegegrad) 1, a care service may also use it to help, for example, with personal hygiene.
pfl.pu.entl.m0: Also for day and night care or short-term care, for example for the personal contribution.
pfl.pu.entl.m1: A family relief service (Familienentlastender Dienst, FED) can also be paid this way if it is recognised in your federal state. These are services that give families with a relative with a disability relief for a few hours, for example with supervision.
pfl.pu.entl.m2: Unused amounts add up. What is left at the end of the year you can still use until 30 June of the following year.
pfl.pu.verh.t: Replacement when the carer is unavailable (Verhinderungs- und Kurzzeitpflege)
pfl.pu.verh.x: One joint budget per year for both. No money into the account: the Pflegekasse uses it to pay for the replacement.
pfl.pu.verh.m0: Respite care (Verhinderungspflege): the carer is on holiday, ill or needs a break. Then someone else provides care at home, for example a care service, an individual carer or volunteers. At most 8 weeks a year.
pfl.pu.verh.m1: This is also possible for a few hours, for example for an afternoon. Hourly supervision is offered among others by family relief services. Payment as Verhinderungspflege is possible: ask the Pflegekasse beforehand.
pfl.pu.verh.m2: Short-term care (Kurzzeitpflege): the person cared for lives in a care facility for a while, for example after hospital. At most 8 weeks a year.
pfl.pu.verh.m3: During the replacement, the Pflegekasse continues to pay half of the Pflegegeld for up to 8 weeks a year.
pfl.pu.verh.m4: If close relatives or people from the same household provide the replacement (not professionally), the Pflegekasse pays at most twice the monthly Pflegegeld. Proven costs such as travel or loss of earnings can be added (up to the annual amount).
pfl.pu.verh.m5: Keep the invoices: you can apply for reimbursement afterwards, at the latest by the end of the following year.
pfl.pu.tages.t: Day care or night care (teilstationäre Pflege)
pfl.pu.tages.x: The person spends the day or the night in a facility. The facility bills the Pflegekasse directly up to this amount.
pfl.pu.tages.m0: Available in addition: Pflegegeld and the care service are not reduced for it.
pfl.pu.tages.m1: Transport to the facility is included. You pay for food and accommodation yourself; the Entlastungsbetrag can help with this.
pfl.pu.kombi.x: If the care service uses only part of its budget, the rest is paid proportionally as Pflegegeld into the account.
pfl.pu.kombi.m0: Example care level (Pflegegrad) {pg}: the care service uses half ({halb}). Then {rest} Pflegegeld a month is still paid into the account.
pfl.pu.kombi.w: You are bound to the split for 6 months.
pfl.pu.hilfs.t: Care box with gloves and more (Pflegehilfsmittel zum Verbrauch)
pfl.pu.hilfs.x: For example disposable gloves, disinfectant or bed protection. Usually a delivery comes, and the provider bills the Pflegekasse.
pfl.pu.hilfs.m0: A care bed is usually provided on loan; you apply for it at the Pflegekasse.
pfl.pu.notruf.t: Emergency call button for the home (Hausnotruf)
pfl.pu.notruf.x: A subsidy from the Pflegekasse is possible if the person is often alone and must be able to call for help in an emergency.
pfl.pu.umbau.x: Subsidy for example for a level-access shower, grab bars or a stairlift. Important: apply before the work, with a cost estimate.
pfl.pu.umbau.m0: If several people in need of care live together, each person gets the subsidy, together up to four times the amount.
pfl.pu.wg.x: For a care shared flat with at least 3 people in need of care and a jointly hired person for everyday life and organisation (Präsenzkraft). The money is meant for this person.
pfl.pu.kurs.x: Learning to provide care, for example lifting and positioning correctly. Also possible at home. Free of charge, even without a care level (Pflegegrad).
pfl.pu.beratung.x: At the Pflegekasse or at the care advice centre (Pflegestützpunkt). They help there with the application and with planning the help.
pfl.pu.beratung.m0: Everyone who receives or has applied for benefits is entitled to Pflegeberatung. Relatives can take part.
pfl.pu.rente.x: Anyone who provides unpaid care for at least 10 hours a week on at least 2 days and works at most 30 hours a week: the Pflegekasse pays pension contributions. This earns pension points.
pfl.pu.rente.m0: How much depends on the care level (Pflegegrad) and on whether Pflegegeld, a care service or both are used. Register the carer with the Pflegekasse; it checks this.
pfl.pu.zeit.t: Time off work for care (Pflegezeit, Familienpflegezeit)
pfl.pu.zeit.x: Up to 10 working days off if care suddenly has to be organised, with care support allowance (Pflegeunterstützungsgeld). Pflegezeit up to 6 months, Familienpflegezeit up to 24 months.
pfl.pu.zeit.m0: Pflegezeit and Familienpflegezeit apply only in larger companies. Ask your employer.
pfl.pu.wer.h: Who provides care? You can choose:
pfl.pu.wer.geld: Family, friends or neighbours provide care
pfl.pu.zusatz.h: In addition (no money into the account, the Pflegekasse pays invoices):
pfl.pu.h: What there is with care level (Pflegegrad) {pg}
pfl.pu.h0: What there is without a care level (Pflegegrad)
pfl.pu.einl2: Most of it is budgets: the care insurance fund (Pflegekasse) uses them to pay for help, usually against an invoice.
pfl.pu.einl2.h: What is paid into the account?
pfl.pu.einl2.m0: Only Pflegegeld and, for people living in an outpatient-supported shared flat, the Wohngruppenzuschlag are paid into the account. Anyone who does not use the budgets gives away help.
pfl.pu.einl1: With care level (Pflegegrad) 1 there is no Pflegegeld yet and no care service as a benefit in kind.
pfl.pu.einl1.m0: But there are budgets and subsidies. The Pflegekasse uses them to pay for help, usually against an invoice.
pfl.pu.einl0: Money and budgets from the care insurance fund (Pflegekasse) only come with a care level (Pflegegrad); this help is available before that.
pfl.pu.einl0.h: How do I get a care level (Pflegegrad)?
pfl.pu.einl0.m0: You apply at the Pflegekasse; a phone call is enough.
pfl.pu.einl0.m1: If the need for care arises suddenly, relatives may stay away from work for up to 10 working days to organise the care. This applies already when a care level is expected. As wage replacement, the Pflegekasse pays the care support allowance (Pflegeunterstützungsgeld) on application.
pfl.pu.stand: Amounts as of: {stand} ({quelle}). The exact entitlement is set by the Pflegekasse.
pfl.pi.h: How the benefits of the care insurance fund (Pflegekasse) work
pfl.pi.lead: Only Pflegegeld and, for people living in an outpatient-supported shared flat, the Wohngruppenzuschlag are paid into the account. Everything else is budgets: the Pflegekasse uses them to pay for help, services or deliveries, usually against an invoice. Anyone who does not use the budgets gives away money.
pfl.pi.z.dienst.w: The care service bills the Pflegekasse directly
pfl.pi.z.entl.w: The Pflegekasse pays invoices from recognised providers
pfl.pi.z.verh: Respite and short-term care (Verhinderungs- und Kurzzeitpflege)
pfl.pi.z.verh.w: For the replacement when the carer is unavailable
pfl.pi.z.verh.h: together {betrag} a year, from care level (Pflegegrad) 2
pfl.pi.z.tages: Day and night care (Tages- und Nachtpflege)
pfl.pi.z.hilfs: Care aids for consumption (Pflegehilfsmittel zum Verbrauch)
pfl.pi.z.hilfs.w: Delivery, for example as a care box
pfl.pi.geld.h: Pflegegeld: money for care by relatives
pfl.pi.geld.0: If relatives, friends or neighbours provide care, the Pflegekasse pays Pflegegeld every month from care level (Pflegegrad) 2 into the account of the person cared for. They can decide freely what to use it for, for example as a thank-you to the carer.
pfl.pi.geld.1: Compulsory: with care levels 2 to 5, a free advice visit comes to the home once every six months. With care levels 4 and 5 this is also possible every quarter on request. If the compulsory advice does not take place, the Pflegekasse can reduce the Pflegegeld.
pfl.pi.dienst.h: Care service: benefit in kind and combination
pfl.pi.dienst.0: If a care service comes, it bills the Pflegekasse directly. You get no money for it, but also no invoice, as long as the budget is enough.
pfl.pi.dienst.1: If the care service uses only part of the budget, the Pflegekasse pays out the rest proportionally as Pflegegeld. This is called Kombinationsleistung.
pfl.pi.entl.h: Entlastungsbetrag: {betrag} a month, but not into the account
pfl.pi.entl.0: The Entlastungsbetrag is available from care level (Pflegegrad) 1. It is not paid out. The Pflegekasse uses it to pay for help that gives the carer relief.
pfl.pi.entl.1: How it works: the provider bills the Pflegekasse directly, or you pay yourself and send in the invoice for reimbursement. The provider must be recognised in your federal state. The Pflegekasse has a list.
pfl.pi.entl.2: Unused amounts add up. You can use them until 30 June of the following year; after that they expire.
pfl.pi.entl.l0: Household help, shopping, accompaniment to the doctor
pfl.pi.entl.l1: Supervision at home or in a supervision group
pfl.pi.entl.l2: Personal contributions for day care or short-term care
pfl.pi.verh.h: Verhinderungspflege and Kurzzeitpflege: replacement for the carer
pfl.pi.verh.0: From care level (Pflegegrad) 2, both share a joint annual amount of {betrag}. This is not money into the account either: the Pflegekasse uses it to pay for the replacement.
pfl.pi.verh.1: Verhinderungspflege: the carer goes on holiday, is ill or needs a few hours' break. Then someone else provides care at home, for example a care service, acquaintances or neighbours.
pfl.pi.verh.2: If close relatives or people from the same household provide the replacement (not professionally), the Pflegekasse pays at most twice the monthly Pflegegeld. Proven costs such as travel or loss of earnings can be added (up to the annual amount).
pfl.pi.verh.3: Kurzzeitpflege: the person cared for lives in a care facility for a while, for example after a hospital stay.
pfl.pi.verh.4: During the replacement, the Pflegekasse continues to pay half of the Pflegegeld for up to 8 weeks a year. If the replacement is only for a few hours (less than 8 hours a day), the full Pflegegeld can continue. Ask your Pflegekasse about this.
pfl.pi.verh.5: Tip: you can also apply afterwards, at the latest by the end of the following year. Keep all invoices and receipts.
pfl.pi.hilfs.h: Care aids and adapting the home
pfl.pi.hilfs.0: Care aids for consumption, for example disposable gloves, disinfectant or bed protection, are available up to {betrag} a month. Usually a box comes to the home, which the provider bills to the Pflegekasse.
pfl.pi.hilfs.1: Larger aids such as a care bed or a walker are usually provided on loan.
pfl.pi.hilfs.2: For adapting the home, for example a level-access shower or grab bars, there is up to {betrag} per measure. Important: apply before the work, with a cost estimate.
pfl.pi.gut.h: Good to know for family carers
pfl.pi.gut.0: Anyone who provides care for at least 10 hours a week on at least 2 days and works at most 30 hours: the Pflegekasse pays pension contributions for them.
pfl.pi.gut.1: In the tax return there is the carer's lump sum (Pflege-Pauschbetrag).
pfl.pi.gut.2: Care advice (Pflegeberatung) is free of charge, at the Pflegekasse or at the care advice centre (Pflegestützpunkt). They also help there with the application.
pfl.pi.stand: Amounts as of: {stand}. The exact entitlement is set by the Pflegekasse.
